title: Toronto police officer faces third charge in death of suicidal teen in park
article: The director of the province's Special Investigation Unit has had a third charge laid against a Toronto police officer in relation to the death of a suicidal teen earlier this year.
The police watchdog agency says a man sought the assistance of a police officer on Feb. 2, 2016, regarding a suicide attempt by another man in Toronto's High Park.
The SIU says the suicidal 19-year-old man was pronounced dead an hour and a half later.
Const. Kyle Upjohn was charged in June with criminal negligence causing death and failing to provide the necessaries of life.
Upjohn appeared in court Thursday to face those charges and an additional charge of breach of trust by a public officer.
The SIU is an arm's length agency that investigates reports involving police where there has been death, serious injury or allegations of sexual assault.
A Toronto police officer is facing criminal charges in connection with a teenager's suicide four months ago.
On Thursday, Ontario's Special Investigations Unit (SIU) announced charges of criminal negligence causing death and failing to provide the necessaries of life against Constable Kyle Upjohn.
Both charges are rare in criminal cases against officers.
The SIU, which investigates all deaths and injuries involving Ontario police officers, has provided only a rough outline of the events.
The agency alleges that around 2 p.m. on Feb. 2, 2015, a man tracked down a Toronto police officer to report an encounter with a suicidal male in High Park.
An hour and a half later, the suicidal male, age 19, was dead.
What unfolded during that interval is now the subject of criminal proceedings. The SIU declined further comment on the case.
Constable Upjohn will appear in court on Aug. 4.
Criminal negligence causing death carries a maximum sentence of life and the second charge can lead to a maximum five-year sentence.

Charges of failing to provide the necessaries of life are rare, but not unprecedented, in SIU cases. Former SIU director Ian Scott recalled prosecuting a similar charge in the Kenora area two decades ago.

"Once a police officer, much like a correctional officer, has someone in custody, they have a set of duties under the law," said Mr. Scott, who has no direct knowledge of the case. "They cannot permit the person to suffer injury or death that they could avoid. It's almost like you're a parent in those circumstances."

But the SIU release does not clarify whether the deceased was ever in police custody. In theory, the charges could still stand, according to Mr. Scott. "Assume for a moment that a police officer was put on notice and then went over and watched while a person committed suicide right in front of them. Possibly I could support those charges. But it seems really odd. Why would any officer do that? There must be some unusual facts here for this charge to have been laid."
Representatives of the Toronto Police Association, the union representing officers in the city, were unavailable for comment.
